# Qwen report inputs and outputs, for review

Every model call that produced a **report** is shown below as what went in and what came out, unedited. This is the expensive periodic tier; `docs/qwen-inputs-and-outputs.md` is the same artifact for the cheap **beat** tier.

| | |
|---|---|
| generated | 2026-08-11 |
| commit | `f43e600` |
| model | Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 Q4_K_M, on device, ctx 8192, temperature 0 |
| corpus snapshot (pinned) | `/home/dg/keld/study-corpus-snapshot-2026-08-11T2130/projects` |
| this harness's own session | `43492104-1861-4682-9890-506bd7f41e67` |
| prompt budget | 14000 characters |
| conversation-window floor | 1600 runes of content |
| report cadence | windows [4 8 12 15] of each session (4 reports) |
| beat cadence | one beat every 5 user turns |
| beats a report may read | at most 12, chosen by SelectBeats |
| retain-list caps | 60 entries / 700 runes |
| distinctiveness table | 33 corpus sessions, 20778 distinct terms, representative=true |
| sessions shown | 16: 14 from the pinned corpus, 2 hand-authored non-engineering |
| reports shown | 128 (each session: 4 reports x 2 arms) |

**The two arms.** They differ in exactly one thing: whether a report whose subject was measured
to have changed is TOLD so.

- **anchor ON** — when the trigger measures a subject shift, the prompt carries the recency
  anchor: what the newest turns are about, plus an instruction to re-scope the synopsis.
- **anchor OFF** — the prompt is always told the refresh was routine, whatever the trigger
  measured.

The measured record is identical in both arms (the trigger reason still feeds the record's
turning points in both), so nothing else moves between them.

**Inputs are labelled by truth status, because that separation is the whole design.**

- **The measured record** is counted on device from the transcript. It is authoritative: the
  prompt says so, and the report is required to be consistent with it.
- **The beat series** is model-generated. It is indicative history — a paraphrase, not evidence
  — and a report may not treat it as fact.
- **The retain-list** is derived deterministically from the previous report's own text. It is
  the only channel carrying a prior report's specifics forward, and every entry is something
  the report is obliged to still carry.
- **The session view and the new turns** are raw transcript, clipped to fit. Where a clip
  happened its notice is shown verbatim rather than elided, because a silently shorter input is
  the same defect one level up.

**What "as included" means.** The conversation window is the value the prompt builder itself
produced. The beat series and the session view are recovered by testing which real
`SelectBeats`/`RenderBeats` and `clipSessionViewFor` output the assembled prompt
contains — not by parsing the prompt between headings, which conversation text quoting a
heading defeats.

**Prompt sizes are observed on the assembled string**, not derived from a bound the code is
supposed to enforce. Failures are shown in place, labelled, with their attempt count — a
refusal, an exhausted retry ladder, a recovered budget panic, or an open list the model left
empty that code then filled. The counts at the end say how many of each this run produced.

**How the pinning was confirmed rather than assumed.** Each session prints the transcript it was
mined from, and every corpus one is under the snapshot path above — session selection reads
`corpusRoot()` now, which it did not before `ad55212`, when a pinned run still
selected sessions from the live, growing directory. The distinctiveness table above was built
from the same root.

**The two hand-authored non-engineering sessions come first** (a month-end close and a product
launch). They are here because the audience requirement is that a non-technical org admin can
read the work out of Atlas, and a file of nothing but code sessions cannot support a judgement
about that.

**Order:** session, then arm, then report step.

**synopsis** (550 runes)

> The March close for the Meridian entity is underway, with the bank reconciliation completed and a residual difference of 1,400.00 remaining unexplained. Four items in transit have been identified and accounted for, including two outstanding cheques, a deposit in transit, and a bank fee. The work is now focused on resolving the remaining discrepancy, which requires deeper analysis of other financial components. The process is structured as a checklist with multiple interdependent steps, and only the bank reconciliation has been finalized so far.

**done** (413 runes)

> The bank reconciliation for March has been completed, identifying a difference of 1,650.55 between the bank statement and ledger cash account. Four items in transit have been identified: two outstanding cheques to Halberd Supply (890.00 and 412.55), a deposit in transit of 1,200.00, and a bank fee of 148.00 not journaled. The reconciliation calculation has been verified and adjusted to account for these items.

**happened** (635 runes)

> The initial reconciliation revealed a discrepancy of 1,650.55, which was attributed to four items in transit. After identifying the outstanding cheques, deposit in transit, and unjournaled bank fee, the assistant recalculated the reconciliation and found a residual difference of 1,400.00, prompting further investigation. The user confirmed the deposit in transit was incorrectly assumed to have cleared, and the assistant clarified its status as a post-cutoff deposit, correctly classifying it as a deposit in transit. The final reconciliation calculation was adjusted to reflect this, but the residual difference remains unresolved.

**structure** (506 runes)

> The close process for the Meridian entity follows a checklist with eight sequential steps: bank reconciliation, AR ageing, AP accruals, payroll journal, intercompany adjustments, fixed asset depreciation, revenue cutoff, and trial balance review. The bank reconciliation is the first step and is currently in progress, with the remaining steps uncompleted. The steps are interdependent, as unresolved items in one area (e.g., bank reconciliation) may impact the accuracy of subsequent financial statements.

**insights** (3 entries)

1. A deposit received after the cut-off must be treated as a deposit in transit, not as a cleared transaction in the ledger.
2. Bank fees posted by the bank but not journaled in the ledger are a common source of reconciliation discrepancies and must be explicitly identified and recorded.
3. The presence of a residual difference after adjusting for in-transit items indicates that further investigation is required beyond the initial reconciliation steps.

**current** (19 runes)

> nothing in progress

**why** (229 runes)

> To ensure accurate financial reporting for the Meridian entity by closing out March with a complete and reconciled set of financial records, including proper identification and treatment of all discrepancies and in-transit items.

**next** (326 runes)

> The team must investigate the remaining difference of 1,400.00 to determine its source, possibly through review of AR, AP, or intercompany transactions. The checklist indicates that AR ageing, AP accruals, payroll journal, intercompany, fixed asset depreciation, revenue cutoff, and trial balance review are pending for March.

**unresolved** (2 entries)

1. A residual difference of 1,400.00 remains unexplained after adjusting for the four items in transit.
2. The AR ageing, AP accruals, payroll journal, intercompany, fixed asset depreciation, revenue cutoff, and trial balance review steps are not yet completed and are pending further work.

**insights** (10 entries)

1. A deposit received after the cut-off must be treated as a deposit in transit, not as a cleared transaction in the ledger.
2. Bank fees posted by the bank but not journaled in the ledger are a common source of reconciliation discrepancies and must be explicitly identified and recorded.
3. The presence of a residual difference after adjusting for in-transit items indicates that further investigation is required beyond the initial reconciliation steps.
4. A duplicate invoice can be detected by checking for two postings of the same amount on different dates without a matching bank debit.
5. Policy adherence must be enforced consistently, even when individual customer risks appear high — deviation can create audit exposure.
6. A blanket policy application to over-90-day receivables avoids audit findings by not creating specific provisions for individual customers.
7. Accruals for goods received but not invoiced must be reviewed by service period, not just by invoice date, to ensure accurate month-end allocation.
8. The Larkin Facilities accrual is quarterly and spans February through April, so only one third of the total accrual belongs in March, not the full amount.
9. A provision of 50% on Northwind’s over-90-day receivable is consistent with policy and has been applied correctly.
10. Payroll journal overpayments must be documented as receivables with recovery timelines to avoid misstatement of liabilities.

**synopsis** (553 runes)

> The campaign plan for Fieldnote is centered on solving the problem of lost field data in environmental and surveying consultancies with 10 to 50 staff. It is built on a clear proof point — the offline-first sync model that ensures fieldwork arrives intact at the office — and is delivered through trusted channels: professional institution newsletters, two industry conferences, and regional practitioner forums. The plan includes a five-email sequence that avoids marketing language and instead tells real stories of fieldwork challenges and solutions.

**done** (742 runes)

> A campaign plan for Fieldnote has been developed with two distinct messaging tracks: one for individual fieldworkers emphasizing durability in harsh conditions, and one for consultancies emphasizing intact data transfer. The outreach strategy is defined across three channels: professional institution newsletters (chartered surveyor and ecological institutions), two industry conferences (autumn surveying congress and regional ecology forum), and regional practitioner forums. A five-email sequence has been drafted and reviewed, with no marketing language, focusing on real-world use cases and narrative storytelling. The outreach to the surveyor firm that lost a week of data has been approved and assigned to deliver the story firsthand.

**happened** (973 runes)

> The initial plan included paid search acquisition, but it was rejected due to high competition and low viability at 8,000 paid search spend. The team pivoted to organic channels where the target audience already gathers. The user initially asked for specific institutions and conferences, prompting detailed follow-up. The assistant identified and confirmed two key institutions: the chartered surveyor institution (12,000 members, $1,400 sponsorship) and the ecological institution (4,000 members, $600 sponsorship), both of which are read rather than filed. Two conferences were identified: the autumn surveying congress (2,200 attendees, small-stand rate) and the regional ecology forum (350 attendees, speaking slot). The speaking slot was prioritized due to higher trust in practitioner-led content. A correction was made to the outreach plan: the story of the surveyor firm losing a week of data is now to be delivered by a fieldworker from that firm, not a marketer.

**structure** (875 runes)

> The campaign is structured around two core audiences: individual fieldworkers and environmental/consultancy firms. For individual users, the message emphasizes resilience in field conditions — rain, gloves, no signal. For consultancies, the message centers on data integrity: fieldwork arriving intact at the office. The outreach is distributed across three channels: (1) professional institution newsletters (chartered surveyor and ecological institutions), (2) two industry conferences (autumn surveying congress and regional ecology forum), and (3) regional practitioner forums. The email sequence consists of five non-marketing emails: (1) the lost-week story, (2) offline capture in no-signal conditions, (3) structured office-side data, (4) a working surveyor’s fortnight, and (5) a plain trial invitation. All messaging avoids urgency, discounts, or exclamation marks.

**insights** (7 entries)

1. The most powerful narrative for consultancies is not the tool’s functionality, but the tangible consequence of data loss — a week of lost work that can cripple operations.
2. Audience segmentation by buyer role (individual vs. consultancy) is essential and must be reflected in messaging and channel targeting.

> Fieldnote’s marketing launch is structured around two primary user paths: the consultancy path, which leads every channel and owns the email sequence, and the individual path, which functions as a self-serve trial accessible from forums. The consultancy narrative emphasizes the offline-first sync model and the protection of field data, with a clear proof point of data integrity across weeks of fieldwork. The individual path is present but not the headline, serving as a low-friction entry point for users who may later bring the tool into their firm. The campaign is supported by a minimal landing page with a one-line problem statement, a 15-second demo, the offline claim, and a trial button. Success is measured through three distinct, non-impression-based metrics: source-tracked trials, trial-to-team conversion, and field retention in week three.

**insights** (12 entries)

1. Organic channels where professionals already gather are more effective than paid acquisition for this niche, especially with limited budgets.
2. The audience for Fieldnote is best reached through trusted, real-world narratives — especially those from practitioners who have experienced data loss.
3. Professional institutions' newsletters are more effective than paid search because the audience reads them, not just files them, creating a higher engagement potential.
4. A speaking slot at a conference is more impactful than a stand because practitioners trust peer-led fieldwork stories over branded displays.
5. The offline-first sync model is not just a feature — it is the core proof point that differentiates Fieldnote from existing tools in consultancies.
6. The consultancy angle is the primary driver of customer acquisition, as most early adopters began as individuals who later brought the tool into their firms.
7. A narrative that centers on real-world fieldwork continuity — not product features — builds stronger trust and authenticity.
8. The individual track must remain but be clearly secondary to the consultancy narrative to avoid diluting the core message.
9. The individual-to-consultancy path is the origin of early customer adoption and must be preserved as a secondary, self-serve trial route.
10. The audience for Fieldnote is not just surveyors or ecologists, but consultancies with 10–50 staff who rely on reliable data transfer from fieldwork.
11. A tool that is abandoned by week three has not been adopted at all — field retention is a more meaningful metric than trial volume.
12. The landing page must prioritize the demonstration over any copy, as the audience detects inauthenticity immediately.

5. A context size of 3072 tokens is sufficient for the real-world window size distribution, providing headroom without unnecessary memory or latency cost.
6. The 4B model's high memory footprint under default settings was due to parallelism and context size, not inherent performance — reducing both context and parallelism brings it within reach of the 1.7B model in efficiency.

## Cost: resolved, and favourably

**Qwen3-0.6B CPU-only with `--cache-ram 512`: 1,463 MB sustained, flat, `validity=1.000`.** That's **49% less RAM than the GLiNER2 you ship**, with a **better p95** (12.2s vs 17.8s) and a marginally worse p50 (8.3s vs 6.8s). No recycle machinery needed — the curve held 1,439–1,510 MB across 80 sustained windows.

The root cause was `--cache-ram` defaulting to **8192 MiB** — a prompt-prefix cache that fills with request count and plateaus at its budget. That single flag explains every ~9 GB reading, why the number was independent of model size, and why `--no-repack`, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` and `--batch-size` all failed to move it.

## Cost: resolved, and favourably

**Qwen3-0.6B CPU-only with `--cache-ram 512`: 1,463 MB sustained, flat, `validity=1.000`.** That's **49% less RAM than the GLiNER2 you ship**, with a **better p95** (12.2s vs 17.8s) and a marginally worse p50 (8.3s vs 6.8s). No recycle machinery needed — the curve held 1,439–1,510 MB across 80 sustained windows.

**Agreement isn't correctness** — none of this says who's right, only adjudication does. But the *pattern* is structured and tells us where to look:

**1. `domain` shows the clean "encoder is the outlier" signature.** The two LLMs agree with each other **86%** while each agrees with GLiNER2 only ~55%. **synopsis** (549 runes)

> This work evaluates CPU-only LLMs for structured classification of chat transcripts, now focused on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B under a bounded prompt cache (`--cache-ram 512`). It grew out of an initial misattribution of memory usage to model size, which was corrected by identifying the default 8192 MiB prompt cache as the root cause. The work now stands on a corrected, stable foundation with clear advantages in RAM efficiency and sustained performance over GLiNER2, and is moving toward a full accuracy comparison in the final adjudication step.

**done** (399 runes)

> Resolved the RAM footprint and latency misestimates in Qwen3-0.6B CPU-only by identifying and fixing the default `--cache-ram 8192` prompt cache as the root cause. Confirmed sustained RAM usage at 1,458–1,519 MB with flat profile. Validated that `--cache-ram` is the dominant memory knob, not `--batch-size`. Corrected and retired stale performance tables and flawed conclusions from early analysis.

**happened** (558 runes)

> Initial analysis incorrectly attributed high RAM usage to model size and `--batch-size`, leading to a misjudged performance profile. The root cause was identified as the unbounded default prompt cache (`--cache-ram 8192`) growing with request count, independent of model size. This caused inflated memory readings and false conclusions about model scalability. The fix involved setting `--cache-ram 512` and re-running benchmarks. Early claims about Qwen3-4B being infeasible were withdrawn due to reliance on pre-plateau data and unbounded cache conditions.

**structure** (685 runes)

> The work centers on evaluating CPU-only LLMs for structured classification of chat transcripts using a moving window of the latest K turns. The system uses a compacted tool use history and summarized code blocks. Models tested include Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-4B, all evaluated under `--cache-ram 512` to control memory. The classification output is compared against GLiNER2's results using structured labels from `labels.go`. The benchmarking pipeline includes CPU memory (RSS), latency, and agreement rates across facets like `task_type`, `domain`, `activity_type`, and `subcategory`. The work is structured around memory efficiency, latency, and classification consistency.

**insights** (12 entries)

1. A hard character cap on turns prevents any single turn from dominating the window, ensuring balanced and manageable input size.
2. The default 'thinking' mode in Qwen3-1.7B introduces significant token overhead that is not reflective of its base model size, and must be disabled for accurate performance comparison.
3. A context size of 3072 tokens is sufficient for the real-world window size distribution, providing headroom without unnecessary memory or latency cost.
4. The 4B model's high memory footprint under default settings was due to parallelism and context size, not inherent performance — reducing both context and parallelism brings it within reach of the 1.7B model in efficiency.
5. LLM-based classification on CPU is now demonstrably more memory-efficient than GLiNER2 under comparable conditions, with 1,841 MB vs 2,894 MB steady state memory usage.
6. A small binary delta (108 KB) from a build tag is negligible and does not justify adding a visible flag, especially when the core functionality is already unguarded.
7. An assumption about system state can fail silently — in this case, a silent overwrite during restore was only detected through explicit verification, reinforcing the need for such checks in automated workflows.
8. Chaining model runs (0.6B → 1.7B) enables end-to-end unattended execution, reducing human intervention and enabling consistent, repeatable evaluation.
9. The default prompt cache (`--cache-ram 8192`) dominates memory usage and is independent of model size, explaining why RAM usage was consistently high across different LLMs.
10. Agreement between LLMs and GLiNER2 on `domain` (86%) suggests GLiNER2 may be the noisy baseline, while low agreement on `activity_type` indicates label ambiguity rather than model deficiency.
11. Qwen3-0.6B with `--cache-ram 512` outperforms GLiNER2 in RAM usage (49% less) and latency (better p95), with stable, flat memory over sustained load.
12. The `--batch-size` knob is not the primary driver of memory; `--cache-ram` is the dominant factor, correcting a prior misattribution.

**current** (189 runes)

> Running Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B at `--cache-ram 512` in a sustained, long-run test with 200 windows; 0.6B has completed 180/200 windows with stable RAM and latency, and 1.7B is following.

**why** (246 runes)

> To identify lightweight, CPU-compatible LLMs that can perform structured classification of chat transcripts with low memory and latency, offering a viable alternative to GPU-dependent models like GLiNER2 without sacrificing accuracy or stability.

**happened** (555 runes)

> Initial configuration with 8192 context and parallel 4 led to high memory usage (8.8 GB) and misaligned performance expectations. Identified that the 1.7B model with thinking enabled consumed excessive tokens and RAM due to default reasoning. Corrected by disabling reasoning in Qwen3-1.7B and re-measuring. Confirmed that the 4B model with ctx 3072 and parallel 1 uses 1,841 MB steady state RAM, below GLiNER2's 2,894 MB.

**structure** (687 runes)

> The work centers on evaluating small, CPU-only LLMs for structured classification of chat transcripts using a moving window of the latest K turns. The system uses a compacted context window that includes tool uses and code blocks, summarized via a window miner. The evaluation compares Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B models against GLiNER2 in terms of memory usage, latency, and classification performance. The architecture includes a synthetic windowing mechanism that aggregates recent turns, a tool use summarization pipeline, and a benchmarking framework that measures RSS and p50/p95 latency. Raw results are stored in `~/.keld/study/run-qwen3-4b.json` and processed into readable metrics.

3. A hard character cap on turns prevents any single turn from dominating the window, ensuring balanced and manageable input size.
4. The default `--parallel 4` setting in llama-server allocates KV cache four times over, creating unnecessary memory overhead that contradicts the single-flight design principle.
5. Context size of 8192 was significantly oversized for the actual window size distribution, with p50 and p95 limits at 523 and 1,000 tokens respectively, making 3072 a more efficient and realistic choice.
6. Qwen3-1.7B's default 'thinking' mode consumes 512 tokens of reasoning per query, which is discarded and inflates both memory and latency — this behavior was misinterpreted as a size effect and must be accounted for in future evaluations.
7. The LLM-based approach with optimized settings (4B, ctx 3072, parallel 1) is more memory-efficient than GLiNER2 under steady-state conditions, with 1,841 MB vs 2,894 MB steady state RAM and 2,564 MB vs 3,817 MB peak RAM.

**structure** (673 runes)

> The work centers on evaluating small local LLMs for structured classification of chat transcripts using a moving window of the latest K turns. The system includes a window miner validated on 464 real transcripts, a schema and prompts derived from `labels.go`, a constrained llama client with transient retry, and an encoder arm with production input and token caps. Session tier and topic verification are fully implemented. The arms include GLiNER2 (control), Qwen3-4B (GPU reference), and Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B (CPU-only, deployable). The CLI and differ/report components are committed and marked hidden. All components are integrated and running or scheduled to run.

**insights** (10 entries)

1. Tool uses contribute meaningfully to the conversation context and must be retained, even if compacted, because they represent active system interactions.
2. The existing `eval/mine` branch's exclusion of tool uses creates a biased window that fails to represent the full session dynamics.
3. A hard character cap on turns prevents any single turn from dominating the window, ensuring balanced and manageable input size.
4. The default `--parallel 4` setting in llama-server allocates KV cache four times over, creating unnecessary memory overhead that contradicts the single-flight design principle.
5. Context size of 8192 was significantly oversized for the actual window size distribution, with p50 and p95 limits at 523 and 1,000 tokens respectively, making 3072 a more efficient and realistic choice.
6. Qwen3-1.7B's default 'thinking' mode consumes 512 tokens of reasoning per query, which is discarded and inflates both memory and latency — this behavior was misinterpreted as a size effect and must be accounted for in future evaluations.
7. The LLM-based approach with optimized settings (4B, ctx 3072, parallel 1) is more memory-efficient than GLiNER2 under steady-state conditions, with 1,841 MB vs 2,894 MB steady state RAM and 2,564 MB vs 3,817 MB peak RAM.
8. CPU-only execution of Qwen3-4B exceeds 30-second pass budgets and uses 6.6 GB RAM, significantly worse than GLiNER2’s 2.9 GB and 6.8 seconds per window, indicating poor feasibility for real-world deployment.
9. The decision to omit a build tag was based on empirical measurement, not preference, demonstrating that technical decisions should be grounded in observable data.
10. A silent failure during restore due to an interactive prompt highlights the importance of verification in automated workflows.

**why** (235 runes)

## Cost: resolved, and favourably

**Qwen3-0.6B CPU-only with `--cache-ram 512`: 1,463 MB sustained, flat, `validity=1.000`.** That's **49% less RAM than the GLiNER2 you ship**, with a **better p95** (12.2s vs 17.8s) and a marginally worse p50 (8.3s vs 6.8s). No recycle machinery needed — the curve held 1,439–1,510 MB across 80 sustained windows.

The root cause was `--cache-ram` defaulting to **8192 MiB** — a prompt-prefix cache that fills with request count and plateaus at its budget. That single flag explains every ~9 GB reading, why the number was independent of model size, and why `--no-repack`, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` and `--batch-size` all failed to move it.

## What I withdrew rather than quietly leave standing

- **The `--batch-size` conclusion was an artifact.** It rested on two pre-plateau readings.
- **The 4B rejection is no longer evidenced.** I rejected it at 5,500 MB — a pre-plateau figure with the cache unbounded. The conclusion may still hold, but I can't claim it, so the doc says so and flags it for re-test.
- The invalid table is struck through in place rather than deleted, so nobody reads those numbers as settled.

## Running now

The system uses a bounded prompt cache (`--cache-ram`) to control memory usage, with tool calls compacted and code blocks summarized. Models evaluated include Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-4B, benchmarked against GLiNER2. Key components include a CLI interface, a structured output format (labels.go), and a measurement pipeline that tracks RSS, latency, and validity over sustained operation. The evaluation is structured around memory and latency constraints, with a 30-second pass budget and a focus on RAM efficiency.

**insights** (12 entries)

1. The existing `eval/mine` branch's exclusion of tool uses creates a biased window that fails to represent the full session dynamics.
2. A hard character cap on turns prevents any single turn from dominating the window, ensuring balanced and manageable input size.
3. The default `--parallel 4` setting in llama-server allocates KV cache four times over, creating unnecessary memory overhead that contradicts the single-flight design principle.
4. Context size of 8192 was significantly oversized for the actual window size distribution, with p50 and p95 limits at 523 and 1,000 tokens respectively, making 3072 a more efficient and realistic choice.
5. Qwen3-1.7B's default 'thinking' mode consumes 512 tokens of reasoning per query, which is discarded and inflates both memory and latency — this behavior was misinterpreted as a size effect and must be accounted for in future evaluations.
6. The LLM-based approach with optimized settings (4B, ctx 3072, parallel 1) is more memory-efficient than GLiNER2 under steady-state conditions, with 1,841 MB vs 2,894 MB steady state RAM and 2,564 MB vs 3,817 MB peak RAM.
7. CPU-only execution of Qwen3-4B exceeds 30-second pass budgets and uses 6.6 GB RAM, significantly worse than GLiNER2’s 2.9 GB and 6.8 seconds per window, indicating poor feasibility for real-world deployment.
8. The decision to omit a build tag was based on empirical measurement, not preference, demonstrating that technical decisions should be grounded in observable data.
9. A silent failure during restore due to an interactive prompt highlights the importance of verification in automated workflows.
10. The root cause of high RAM usage in earlier evaluations was the unbounded prompt cache (`--cache-ram 8192`), which grows with request count and dominates memory footprint regardless of model size.
11. Agreement patterns between models reveal that `domain` classification shows strong convergence between LLMs and each other, suggesting GLiNER2 may be the outlier with noisy or inconsistent labeling, while `activity_type` shows low agreement across all systems, indicating a vocabulary or labeling ambiguity issue in `labels.go`.
12. Qwen3-0.6B with bounded cache outperforms GLiNER2 in both RAM efficiency and p95 latency, demonstrating a viable, CPU-only alternative for structured classification tasks with minimal hardware requirements.

Apple issues several different certificate *types*, and each one is only valid for signing a specific kind of thing. Two of them are relevant to shipping a `.pkg` outside the App Store:

| Cert type (what you pick in the portal) | What it signs |
|---|---|
| **Developer ID Application** | executables — your `keld`, `keld-agent`, `keld-agent-sidecar` binaries |
| **Developer ID Installer** | the `.pkg` installer file itself |

They are not interchangeable. `productbuild --sign` rejects an Application cert, and `codesign` rejects an Installer cert. So a signed-and-notarized pkg needs both: the binaries inside get signed with Application, then the pkg wrapping them gets signed with Installer.

That's exactly what your build script already assumes:

- `installers/macos/build-pkg.sh:17-21` — signs the three binaries with `$APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_APP`
- `installers/macos/build-pkg.sh:32-34` — signs the pkg with `$APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_INSTALLER`

Two env vars, two certs, two `.p12` files (or one p12 holding both, if you prefer).

Also worth knowing: notarization would fail on an unsigned-binary pkg anyway. Apple requires every Mach-O inside to be signed with hardened runtime — that's the `--options runtime` on line 19.… Logged in as `dgabriele`. Apple issues several different certificate *types*, and each one is only valid for signing a specific kind of thing. Two of them are relevant to shipping a `.pkg` outside the App Store:

| Cert type (what you pick in the portal) | What it signs |
|---|---|
| **Developer ID Application** | executables — your `keld`, `keld-agent`, `keld-agent-sidecar` binaries |
| **Developer ID Installer** | the `.pkg` installer file itself |

They are not interchangeable. `productbuild --sign` rejects an Application cert, and `codesign` rejects an Installer cert. So a signed-and-notarized pkg needs both: the binaries inside get signed with Application, then the pkg wrapping them gets signed with Installer.

- `installers/macos/build-pkg.sh:32-34` — signs the pkg with `$APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_INSTALLER`

Two env vars, two certs, two `.p12` files (or one p12 holding both, if you prefer).

Also worth knowing: notarization would fail on an unsigned-binary pkg anyway. Apple requires every Mach-O inside to be signed with hardened runtime — that's the `--options runtime` on line 19.… Logged in as `dgabriele`. - **Derives the identity names from the keychain** via `security find-identity` instead of reading them from secrets. A mistyped identity name fails at `productsign` time with an unhelpful error; the cert already carries its exact name. `APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_APP`/`_INSTALLER` remain as optional overrides but you don't need to set them.
- Prepends to the keychain search list rather than replacing it — replacing drops the login/System keychains and with them the Apple roots the chain validates against.
- Disables the 5-minute auto-lock (`-lut 21600`); a mid-build relock fails as a "user interaction required" error that reads nothing like its cause.
- Paired `Remove signing keychain` step with `if: always()`.
- Skips cleanly with no cert secrets → unsigned build, as before.

- `.p8` handling: `--key` wants a *path*, so it now accepts either a path or the key contents, writing contents to the trap-cleaned temp dir at `umask 077`.…

**insights** (12 entries)

1. Private keys must be present in the .p12 file; a certificate without a private key is unusable for signing.
2. Deriving identity names from the keychain via `security find-identity` is more reliable than relying on hardcoded or mistyped identity names in secrets.
3. The signing workflow can be tested independently of notary credentials, allowing early detection of issues like incorrect entitlements or partition list errors.
4. Apple’s `.p8` key can be passed directly by content, and the Key ID and Issuer ID are visible on the App Store Connect keys page — the Issuer ID is per-account and often overlooked.
5. A throwaway keychain that preserves system keychains and disables auto-lock prevents build failures due to user interaction prompts or keychain locking.
6. The signing path via curl | sh and sudo installer -pkg bypasses Gatekeeper quarantine entirely, making it a viable fallback for self-hosted or unmanaged environments.
7. Nested Mach-O components — like embedded frameworks — require in-scope signing and are a critical failure point when not properly handled; the fix was to sign all 103 files in the sidecar bundle.
8. Apple's notarization is not a verification mechanism but a chokepoint with rent and unilateral control, which creates a real business risk for developers who rely on user autonomy.
9. The G2 intermediate chain resolves the full certificate path, enabling trust from Apple Root CA and eliminating chain gaps that would have failed validation.
10. The `notarytool submit --wait` step has no timeout and can block indefinitely if Apple's service stalls, risking job timeouts on GitHub's 6-hour limit.
11. Apple's notary queue is slow for large payloads (e.g., 200 MB with 103 signed Mach-O binaries and embedded Python.framework), but this is within expected range for such complexity.
12. The `.p8` credentials and key/issuer/kid values used in the CI workflow are valid and correctly authenticated against Apple's Notary API, confirming that the signing and submission process is secure and properly configured.

assistant: Fair — let me back up.

Apple issues several different certificate *types*, and each one is only valid for signing a specific kind of thing. Two of them are relevant to shipping a `.pkg` outside the App Store:

| Cert type (what you pick in the portal) | What it signs |
|---|---|
| **Developer ID Application** | executables — your `keld`, `keld-agent`, `keld-agent-sidecar` binaries |
| **Developer ID Installer** | the `.pkg` installer file itself |

They are not interchangeable. `productbuild --sign` rejects an Application cert, and `codesign` rejects an Installer cert. So a signed-and-notarized pkg needs both: the binaries inside get signed with Application, then the pkg wrapping them gets signed with Installer.

That's exactly what your build script already assumes:

- `installers/macos/build-pkg.sh:17-21` — signs the three binaries with `$APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_APP`
- `installers/macos/build-pkg.sh:32-34` — signs the pkg with `$APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_INSTALLER`

Two env vars, two certs, two `.p12` files (or one p12 holding both, if you prefer).

Also worth knowing: notarization would fail on an unsigned-binary pkg anyway. Apple requires every Mach-O inside to be signed with hardened runtime — that's the `--options runtime` on line 19.… Logged in as `dgabriele`. Nothing for me to do with that yet — but once you have the two `.p12` files, that's what lets us push the secrets straight from here:

Apple issues several different certificate *types*, and each one is only valid for signing a specific kind of thing. Two of them are relevant to shipping a `.pkg` outside the App Store:

| Cert type (what you pick in the portal) | What it signs |
|---|---|
| **Developer ID Application** | executables — your `keld`, `keld-agent`, `keld-agent-sidecar` binaries |
| **Developer ID Installer** | the `.pkg` installer file itself |

They are not interchangeable. `productbuild --sign` rejects an Application cert, and `codesign` rejects an Installer cert. So a signed-and-notarized pkg needs both: the binaries inside get signed with Application, then the pkg wrapping them gets signed with Installer.

That's exactly what your build script already assumes:

- `installers/macos/build-pkg.sh:17-21` — signs the three binaries with `$APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_APP`
- `installers/macos/build-pkg.sh:32-34` — signs the pkg with `$APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_INSTALLER`

Two env vars, two certs, two `.p12` files (or one p12 holding both, if you prefer).

Also worth knowing: notarization would fail on an unsigned-binary pkg anyway. Apple requires every Mach-O inside to be signed with hardened runtime — that's the `--options runtime` on line 19.… Logged in as `dgabriele`. ## What changed

**`.github/workflows/installers.yml`** — new `Import Apple signing certs` step before packaging:
- Creates a throwaway keychain in `$RUNNER_TEMP`, imports both p12s with `-T /usr/bin/codesign -T /usr/bin/productsign -T /usr/bin/productbuild`, sets the partition list so signing doesn't block on a GUI prompt.
- **Derives the identity names from the keychain** via `security find-identity` instead of reading them from secrets. A mistyped identity name fails at `productsign` time with an unhelpful error; the cert already carries its exact name. `APPLE_DEVELOPER_ID_APP`/`_INSTALLER` remain as optional overrides but you don't need to set them.
- Prepends to the keychain search list rather than replacing it — replacing drops the login/System keychains and with them the Apple roots the chain validates against.
- Disables the 5-minute auto-lock (`-lut 21600`); a mid-build relock fails as a "user interaction required" error that reads nothing like its cause.
- Paired `Remove signing keychain` step with `if: always()`.
- Skips cleanly with no cert secrets → unsigned build, as before.

**`installers/macos/build-pkg.sh`**:
- `.p8` handling: `--key` wants a *path*, so it now accepts either a path or the key contents, writing contents to the trap-cleaned temp dir at `umask 077`.…

**insights** (7 entries)

1. Apple Developer ID certificates must be explicitly selected from the G2 Sub-CA (Xcode 11.4.1 or later) to ensure validity and chain completeness.
2. Self-signed local-machine identities, often generated during macOS keychain operations, are not suitable for distribution signing and will fail in build processes.
3. Certificate type must be correctly matched: Developer ID Application for binaries, Developer ID Installer for the .pkg file itself.
4. Private keys must be present in the .p12 file; a certificate without a private key is unusable for signing.
5. The exact identity name of a certificate is embedded in its keychain entry and can be reliably extracted via `security find-identity`, eliminating the risk of mistyped identity names that previously caused unhelpful errors during `productsign`.
6. A workflow can safely run without notary credentials and still produce a signed package, allowing for independent testing of the signing path before final release.
7. Apple's `.p8` keys can be passed directly by content to scripts, and the Key ID and Issuer ID are available on the App Store Connect page under Users and Access → Integrations → Keys, with the Issuer ID being per-account and easily missed.

**structure** (1142 runes)

> The Signal Client monitoring dashboard is a new sub-project (C) within keld-atlas, built in the `services/admin-web` Next.js 16 / React 19 service. It renders data from B's `/admin/signal/*` endpoints and follows the admin-web flat convention: types and fetch logic in `lib/admin.ts`, one hook file, and pages under `app/(app)/`. The design includes:
> - `/signal` (overview) page: header with window and org filters, fleet summary tiles (installs, events, errors), installs table (with per-severity badges and metrics), and anomaly feed (with severity and code filtering).
> - The dashboard relies on backend endpoints: `/signal/summary`, `/signal/installs`, `/signal/events` (with `min_severity=warn`).
> - Key technical constraints: no shared UI primitives (cards, tables, badges are hand-rolled), no chart library (using recharts as default), and polling at ~30s intervals for near-live updates.
> - Design decisions: overview-first single `/signal` page with install drill-in, full v1 scope (all 5 endpoints), and recharts for resource trend charts. Window-hours and org filters (cross-org by default) are included for platform admin visibility.

**insights** (7 entries)

1. The dashboard design must be grounded in the existing admin-web routing and component patterns before any design decisions are finalized
2. Service updates can be safely performed in sequence — rebuild and restart — without disrupting ongoing telemetry collection
3. The absence of a loaded Gliner2 model is a known state, not a design decision, and does not currently impact the telemetry capture path
4. GLiNER2 model loading is by design — it is lazily loaded per request, not at startup, which reduces resource overhead and aligns with the sidecar's recyclable worker architecture.
5. The admin-web explorer is still active and will provide critical design patterns (routing, component reuse, navigation) needed to shape the dashboard's information architecture and scope.
6. The dashboard will use recharts for resource trend charts, consistent with existing design tokens (`--keld-chart-*`), and will implement polling at ~30s intervals for near-live refreshes.
7. The design defaults to a full v1 scope (all 5 endpoints) and an overview-first `/signal` page with install drill-in and anomaly feed, pending final review.

## Why 100 is fine
Volume math with retention as the governor:
- Gauges dominate: ~288/install/day. 100 installs × 288 ≈ **29k gauge rows/day**; the 30-day gauge sweep caps that at **~865k rows**. Anomalies + lifecycle events are far sparser (90-day retention). Steady state ≈ **~1M narrow rows**.

> The Signal Client monitoring system is built on three interdependent sub-projects:
> - **keld-cli (client capture)**: The `keld-agent` daemon captures client events and posts them to a local API endpoint (`http://localhost:8002/admin/signal`) via `hook.json`.
> - **keld-atlas (ingest and query)**: The backend service ingests events into PostgreSQL, with indexed filters on `install_id`, `event_time`, and `severity` to support filtering and search.
> - **admin-web (dashboard)**: Renders both synthetic seed data and real client events in a live UI, currently using a production build that does not auto-reflect code changes. The anomaly column in the UI requires a manual rebuild to show the fix.
> All components are integrated and functional in a local development environment, with end-to-end validation confirmed.

**insights** (12 entries)

1. The absence of a loaded Gliner2 model is a known state, not a design decision, and does not currently impact the telemetry capture path
2. GLiNER2 model loading is by design — it is lazily loaded per request, not at startup, which reduces resource overhead and aligns with the sidecar's recyclable worker architecture.
3. The admin-web explorer is still active and will provide critical design patterns (routing, component reuse, navigation) needed to shape the dashboard's information architecture and scope.
4. The dashboard will use recharts for resource trend charts, consistent with existing design tokens (`--keld-chart-*`), and will implement polling at ~30s intervals for near-live refreshes.
5. The design defaults to a full v1 scope (all 5 endpoints) and an overview-first `/signal` page with install drill-in and anomaly feed, pending final review.
6. The 'Anomalies' column in the installs table misrepresents `info` events as anomalies, creating confusion — this is a design flaw that must be corrected to align with the actual monitoring intent.
7. Real client events from the local keld-agent daemon are now successfully ingested and appear in the dashboard, confirming the full end-to-end loop from login to event posting and display.
8. The dashboard currently lacks shared UI components (cards, tables, badges), which are hand-rolled — this indicates a need for a shared component library to improve consistency and reduce development effort in future work.
9. PostgreSQL query performance at 100 clients is stable due to retention-based volume caps — the working set remains bounded by ~1M rows, which Postgres can scan in tens of milliseconds.
10. The current indexing strategy (all composite indexes leading with `org_id`) is misaligned with the dashboard’s actual access patterns, causing degradation before 1k clients.
11. Real-time filtering and search performance will degrade as client volume grows because the query predicates do not leverage the full index structure effectively.
12. The admin-web dashboard currently runs a production build (`next start`) without hot-reload, so UI changes (like the anomaly-count fix) require a rebuild to take effect, even though the underlying data refreshes live.

> Assessing the scalability of PostgreSQL queries under 100 signal clients, particularly in the context of real-time filtering and search performance on the admin-web dashboard.

**why** (193 runes)

**synopsis** (480 runes)

> The Signal Client monitoring dashboard is now fully operational in local development, with real client events from a locally running keld-agent daemon being ingested and displayed. **done** (413 runes)

> The Signal Client monitoring dashboard local development environment is fully set up and functional. Real client events from a local keld-agent daemon are now being ingested and displayed in the dashboard. The full end-to-end authentication and event flow (login → setup → hook → event posting) has been verified and closed. The dashboard now shows both synthetic seed data and real events from the local machine.

**happened** (677 runes)

> The initial work focused on setting up the local development environment for the Signal Client monitoring dashboard, including configuring the local API endpoint at `http://localhost:8000` and the admin-web dashboard at `http://localhost:3002/signal`. A user reported seeing 'info 2' under anomalies, which was traced to a UI mislabeling: the backend counts all event severities, including `info`, and the column is incorrectly titled 'Anomalies'. This was resolved by identifying the source of the mislabeling in the frontend code and confirming the behavior. The work progressed smoothly with no major obstacles or reversals, though the UI inaccuracy required a targeted fix.

**structure** (843 runes)

> The Signal Client monitoring dashboard is built on top of the existing admin-web app structure and routing. It uses a local API endpoint (`http://localhost:8000`) to receive client events from the keld-agent daemon via a `hook.json` configuration. The dashboard displays synthetic seed data by default and now also shows real events from the local daemon. The frontend renders events in a table and chart, with the installs table showing per-install event counts. The 'Anomalies' column currently includes all severities, including `info`, which is a mislabeling. The backend (signal_events.py) tallies all events, and the frontend (installs-table.tsx) renders the counts under a misleading header. The dashboard is currently not using any shared UI primitives (cards, tables, badges are hand-rolled), and relies on recharts for visualization.

**insights** (10 entries)

1. The dashboard design must be grounded in the existing admin-web routing and component patterns before any design decisions are finalized
2. Service updates can be safely performed in sequence — rebuild and restart — without disrupting ongoing telemetry collection
3. The absence of a loaded Gliner2 model is a known state, not a design decision, and does not currently impact the telemetry capture path
4. GLiNER2 model loading is by design — it is lazily loaded per request, not at startup, which reduces resource overhead and aligns with the sidecar's recyclable worker architecture.
5. The admin-web explorer is still active and will provide critical design patterns (routing, component reuse, navigation) needed to shape the dashboard's information architecture and scope.
6. The dashboard will use recharts for resource trend charts, consistent with existing design tokens (`--keld-chart-*`), and will implement polling at ~30s intervals for near-live refreshes.
7. The design defaults to a full v1 scope (all 5 endpoints) and an overview-first `/signal` page with install drill-in and anomaly feed, pending final review.
8. The 'Anomalies' column in the installs table misrepresents `info` events as anomalies, creating confusion — this is a design flaw that must be corrected to align with the actual monitoring intent.
9. Real client events from the local keld-agent daemon are now successfully ingested and appear in the dashboard, confirming the full end-to-end loop from login to event posting and display.
10. The dashboard currently lacks shared UI components (cards, tables, badges), which are hand-rolled — this indicates a need for a shared component library to improve consistency and reduce development effort in future work.

**current** (182 runes)

> Fixing the 'Anomalies' column in the installs table to correctly filter only events with severity `warn` or higher, by updating the frontend rendering logic to exclude `info` events.

**why** (244 runes)

> To enable real-time monitoring of client telemetry from the Signal Client, ensuring that operational events (like daemon startup and resource usage) are visible and actionable in a dashboard that reflects actual user behavior and system health.

**next** (325 runes)

## Why 100 is fine
Volume math with retention as the governor:
- Gauges dominate: ~288/install/day. 100 installs × 288 ≈ **29k gauge rows/day**; the 30-day gauge sweep caps that at **~865k rows**. Anomalies + lifecycle events are far sparser (90-day retention). Steady state ≈ **~1M narrow rows**.
- Postgres scans ~1M rows in tens of ms. Even the queries that *can't* use an index (below) finish fast at this size, and the per-install N+1 loop is bounded (≤200 installs/page, and each sub-query *is* index-served). **No problem at 100.**

Retention is the real scalability lever here — as long as that arq sweep runs, the working set stays bounded to `clients × gauge-rate × 30d`.

## The bottlenecks that bite as you grow (ranked)

**1. Index ↔ query mismatch (the big one).** Every composite index *leads with `org_id`*:
- `(org_id, install_id, ts)`, `(org_id, severity, ts)`, `(org_id, code, ts)` — plus a lone `(received_at)`.…

> The Signal Client monitoring dashboard is built on top of the existing admin-web app structure and routing. It relies on a live backend API at http://localhost:8002/admin/signal, which receives events from the keld-agent daemon via its hook.json configuration. The daemon posts events to this endpoint, and the dashboard renders both synthetic seed data and real client events. Data is stored in PostgreSQL with composite indexes on `(org_id, install_id, ts)`, `(org_id, severity, ts)`, and `(org_id, code, ts)`, which are designed to support filtering and search. However, these indexes are misaligned with the actual query patterns used in the dashboard, leading to performance degradation as client volume grows. The anomaly-count logic has been fixed and merged, but requires a dashboard rebuild to appear in the UI. The system is currently stable at 100 clients, with no performance issues observed under real-time filtering and search.

**insights** (12 entries)

1. Service updates can be safely performed in sequence — rebuild and restart — without disrupting ongoing telemetry collection
2. The absence of a loaded Gliner2 model is a known state, not a design decision, and does not currently impact the telemetry capture path
3. GLiNER2 model loading is by design — it is lazily loaded per request, not at startup, which reduces resource overhead and aligns with the sidecar's recyclable worker architecture.
4. The admin-web explorer is still active and will provide critical design patterns (routing, component reuse, navigation) needed to shape the dashboard's information architecture and scope.
5. The dashboard will use recharts for resource trend charts, consistent with existing design tokens (`--keld-chart-*`), and will implement polling at ~30s intervals for near-live refreshes.
6. The design defaults to a full v1 scope (all 5 endpoints) and an overview-first `/signal` page with install drill-in and anomaly feed, pending final review.
7. The 'Anomalies' column in the installs table misrepresents `info` events as anomalies, creating confusion — this is a design flaw that must be corrected to align with the actual monitoring intent.
8. Real client events from the local keld-agent daemon are now successfully ingested and appear in the dashboard, confirming the full end-to-end loop from login to event posting and display.
9. The dashboard currently lacks shared UI components (cards, tables, badges), which are hand-rolled — this indicates a need for a shared component library to improve consistency and reduce development effort in future work.
10. PostgreSQL query performance at 100 signal clients is stable due to retention-based volume caps and efficient indexing, but the current index design is mismatched to real access patterns, causing premature degradation.
11. The daemon's idle CPU and low startup RSS are real metrics, not chart artifacts — the sidecar load is the key driver of resource usage.
12. The admin-web dashboard does not reflect code changes (like the anomaly-count fix) unless explicitly rebuilt, even though the underlying data is live and updated in real time.

| anchor, text v2 | 90.9% | **2.0%** | **0.7%** | 14.3% |

**The design, in short.** Two grains within the session — specific actions (recent window, in detail) and the session story (accumulating, coarsening as it grows). Between them a compression step: the refinement receives a **≤600-rune paraphrase** of the previous digest plus the deterministic retain-list, instead of 4,742 characters of embedded prose. That's your sentence exactly — *"work has been on X, Y, Z; specifically A, B, C"* — with the paraphrase supplying the framing and the retain-list supplying the instances.

**The invariant that makes it safe: store full, feed compressed.** My one hard-won finding is that repeated re-summarization erodes the best content. That still holds, so the lossy path is the *prompt* only. The stored digest is never regenerated from a paraphrase. The spec calls this out as needing a test rather than a convention, because it's the one way this design could quietly destroy the record.

**Three things it deletes.** The "must not become shorter" rule, which directly contradicts deliberate compression. `CarryForward` and the priority scheme deciding which sections yield budget.…
user: But to understand the larger picture of the session, would we not want to consult the summarized/condensed digests at some sampling frequency across the session or at least across a much larger rolling window?
assistant: Yes — and that's a real gap in what I wrote. A single paraphrase of the immediately-previous digest is a chain where each step sees only one step back, which is precisely the telephone risk I listed and then didn't actually mitigate. Consulting a *series* of condensed digests across the session both gives the trajectory and bounds the drift, because a late generation can see where the work started, not just where it was last round.

`digeststore` already keeps every snapshot with its `seq`, so the sequence is there to read.

**The story ladder.** Each refinement now receives a chronological sequence of stored paraphrases rather than just the last:

- **the first, always** — where the work started, so the account can say what the current work grew out of; dropping it is how a session loses its own origin
- **the most recent in full** (≤600 runes) — the immediate handover
- **evenly spaced middles, clipped short** (≤140 runes each) — the trajectory, without paying full price per step
- capped at **8**; beyond that the middles are resampled rather than appended

Dense at the recent end, sparse toward the start — the same shape `SessionDigest` already uses for turns, for the same reason.

**It's cheaper than what it replaces.** Worst case ~1,580 runes against the 4,742 the embedded digest costs, while covering the whole session instead of one step of it. That's the part I'd missed: sampling across the session isn't an added cost, it's what compression pays for.

**And it's the drift bound I claimed but hadn't built.** With a ladder, framing is checkable against the session's *own* earlier framings, so drift is visible to the generation that would otherwise compound it.…

The current design introduces a digest ladder — a sequence of compressed, chronological summaries — that preserves origin, shows trajectory, and bounds drift, enabling accurate, long-term tracking of work progression.

**done** (512 runes)

> 1. A new session-story rollup design has been written and committed to `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-10-session-story-rollup-design.md` (commit `0970391`).
> 2. The design was updated to include a sequence of condensed digests (ladder) across the session, with the first as origin, the most recent as immediate handover, and evenly spaced middle points as trajectory.
> 3. The design explicitly removes the 'must not become shorter' rule and eliminates `CarryForward` and the priority scheme for section budgeting.

**happened** (966 runes)

> The work initially focused on fixing stale blockers in digest generation, where the model was fabricating closure states and misrepresenting open items. This was resolved by implementing a prompt-level accounting rule that tracks open items accurately.
> A key obstacle emerged when the model began over-anchoring to early turns, inventing new fields like tool name and call ID not discussed in the session, indicating subject drift.
> A reversal occurred when the team realized that repeated re-summarization erodes valuable content, leading to a design shift that avoids re-summarization in the prompt.
> A further realization was that a single paraphrase of the previous digest is insufficient to track session drift, so a chronological ladder of condensed digests was introduced to provide trajectory and bound drift.
> Obstacles to implementation included the need to maintain session origin, ensure trajectory visibility, and avoid loss of content through compression.

**structure** (677 runes)

> The work is structured around two core components: (1) specific actions — recent turns detailed in full, and (2) the session story — a coarsening, chronological narrative built from a ladder of condensed digests. Between them is a compression step: each refinement receives a ≤600-rune paraphrase of the previous digest plus a deterministic retain-list, not the full embedded digest. The ladder includes: the first (origin), the most recent (immediate handover), evenly spaced middles (trajectory, clipped to ≤140 runes), capped at 8 total points. This structure ensures that the work's evolution is visible, drift is bounded, and content is preserved without re-summarization.

**insights** (12 entries)

1. Provenance is best expressed through design, not metadata decoration — the structure itself becomes the documentation.
2. The presence of synthetic sessions shows that the work is focused on structural validity rather than factual accuracy.
3. The budget table reveals that the allocation of value to 'happened' is driven by contextual reasoning, not arbitrary thresholds.
4. Recency and retention are in direct tension — no configuration clears T11 lag without increasing the risk of retention loss or fabricated blockers.
5. The model's synopsis subject is unreliable: it either lags on long sessions or over-anchors on short ones, reflecting a lack of dynamic grounding in the present session.
6. The `recurring topics` field is empty in every measurement because the digest path never performs a classification pass — this removes any recency signal from the prompt.
7. The `wordsOf` tokenizer breaks terms with uppercase letters, fragmenting `DigestSchema` into `igest` and `chema`, which undermines schema recognition — a flaw only visible in specific contexts.
8. The model can fabricate details not measured in the data (e.g., inventing fields like 'tool name', 'call ID') because the `unresolved` check does not validate presence of such fields in the input.
9. Repeated re-summarization erodes the most valuable content — insight merging must happen in code, not through model reprocessing.
10. A session-level digest ladder, with origin, recent, and spaced middle points, provides both trajectory and drift detection without requiring full re-summarization.
11. The design achieves compression by feeding a ≤600-rune paraphrase and a deterministic retain-list, reducing prompt size from 4,742 runes to ~1,580 in worst case while preserving session context.
12. The session origin must be preserved — removing it causes the work to lose its own starting point and narrative continuity.

**Two things were wrong beneath the symptom.** First, the facts block was designed to carry `recurring topics` as a recency anchor — but those fields come from `WithEnrichment`, which needs a classification pass the digest path never makes. **They have been empty in every measurement I've taken**, so the prompt had no pull toward the present at all. Second, building the metric needed a third tokenizer: `wordsOf` keeps only `[a-z0-9]`, so uppercase letters are *separators* and it shreds `DigestSchema` into `igest`+`chema` — safe for its existing callers only because they all lowercase first — while `identifierPat` matches no ordinary lowercase word and excludes `/`.

**T11 is now a real threshold**: does the synopsis reflect the session's present, or a subject it left behind? It's the one failure nothing else caught — a lagging synopsis has nothing fabricated (T7 passes) and contradicts nothing (T8 passes). It's just out of date, which is precisely what a reader can't detect.

| anchor, text v1 | 88.3% | 10.2% | 1.7% | **7.1%** |
| anchor, text v2 | 90.9% | **2.0%** | **0.7%** | 14.3% |

              else. Name the subject in the first sentence — not the activity, the
              THING. This is the one section that may draw on the others; it is a
              synthesis, not another status field. Do not restate the purpose sentence
              from "why" — the reader wants the shape of the work, not its justification.
  done        What concrete outcomes are now in place? Name them. Do not describe
              effort or intent here — only what is finished.
  happened    How did it actually go? Include obstacles, wrong turns, reversals, and
              how they were resolved. This is where difficulty belongs.
  structure   How does the thing being worked on fit together? Its parts, what each
              is for, and how they relate. For technical work this is the architecture;
              for other work, the shape of the process. Describe the SUBJECT, not
              the session. Build the fullest picture the conversation supports.
  insights    Key thoughts and learnings. One per entry. Only things a reader could
              not infer from the bare facts.
  current     What single thing is in progress right now? Answer "nothing in
              progress" if the work reached a stopping point.
  why         What purpose does this serve? The goal behind the work — not a
              restatement of what was done.
  next        Where is this going? The direction, plus the concrete immediate steps
              that follow from it.
  unresolved  What is still open, blocked, or was abandoned? One per entry.
              If genuinely NOTHING is open, the entry must be exactly:
                none - the work reached a stopping point
              Do not invent an open item to fill this field. An invented blocker is
              worse than no blocker, because a reader will act on it.

Updating rules:
  - Do not drop earlier material simply because the new part does not mention it — build
    on the beats and the specifics above unless the new part contradicts it. Every named
    specific listed above must still appear, unless the new part shows it was wrong.
    Compression is fine — shorten or drop framing — as long as no named specific and no
    open item is lost doing it.
  - Where something changed, revise it in place and say what changed.
  - synopsis: decide first whether the new part CONTINUES the work the report describes or
    has moved to a different subject. If it continues, keep the subject and framing and
    update only where the work now stands and where it is going. If the subject has genuinely
    moved on, RE-SCOPE it to the work as it now is, and say what it grew out of. A synopsis
    that still describes an abandoned starting point is worse than one that changed, because
    a reader will believe it. Do not re-scope merely because the newest turns are about a
    detail of the same work.
  - structure: EXTEND the picture with newly revealed parts, and correct anything the
    new part shows was wrong. Do not rewrite it from scratch.
  - insights: add only genuinely new learnings. Do not restate existing ones in
    different words — a reworded repeat is still a repeat.
  - retired: list an existing insight here, copied as written, ONLY if the new part shows
    it is WRONG or was reversed. This is for correcting the record, not for tidying it:
    an insight that is merely old, less interesting, or now less relevant stays. Use an
    empty list when nothing was contradicted.
  - unresolved must describe the CURRENT state. An item the new part resolved goes in
    the "closed" list, NOT in unresolved — a reader will act on anything left in
    unresolved, so a resolved item left there costs them real work. Add what has newly
    opened.
  - current names what is underway RIGHT NOW. If the last thing described is finished,
    the answer is "nothing in progress" — do not report a completed action here.

Rules:
  - Report only what the conversation supports. If something is not stated, do not
    assert it. Absence of evidence is itself worth reporting.
  - The COUNTS above are measured facts and your report must be consistent with
    them. If corrections occurred, the work did not go smoothly and the report must
    say so.
  - Name specifics (files, systems, people, amounts) only when they appear in the
    conversation. Do not invent plausible ones.
  - unresolved must be addressed, but only with items the conversation actually
    supports. If the work was verified and nothing remains, use the exact "none -"
    entry above. Never speculate that something "needs further testing" or "is not
    fully understood" unless the conversation says so.
  - Write about the WORK, not about the assistant or the conversation. Describe what
    changed and what state things are in, never who typed what. The reader cares
    what happened to the work, not who did it.
  - Each section must add something the others do not. Do not restate one section's
    content in another. The single exception is synopsis, whose job IS to synthesise —
    but it must still be written, not assembled by copying sentences from elsewhere.
  - The section descriptions above are QUESTIONS to answer, not text to copy. Never
    echo a description back as your answer.
  - Every noun in your report must come from the conversation above. Nothing in
    these instructions is subject matter — do not borrow words from them.

Respond with JSON only.

**synopsis** (484 runes)

> The work is about ensuring that digests accurately reflect the current state of work, not just the most recent turns. The current effort is to redesign the anchor logic and tokenizer to balance recency and retention, while detecting and correcting cases where the synopsis becomes outdated without being fabricated.

**done** (589 runes)

> 1. The fix for stale blockers in digest generation is complete and verified — the prompt-level accounting rule ensures that open items are properly tracked, and the model no longer fabricates or misrepresents closure states. 2. The anchor text configuration has been updated to include the clause 'leave other sections alone', which directly improves retention and reduces fabricated blockers in specific metrics. 3. A new artifact has been generated and made available: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/232bd28f-639a-4bf5-a3f5-b5b04d073c26, containing current digest examples side by side.

**happened** (821 runes)

> The model initially over-anchored to recent turns, causing a drop in retention (T4) and a rise in fabricated blockers (T7). This was traced to two root issues: (1) the facts block relied on `WithEnrichment` fields that were never processed due to missing classification passes, leading to no recency anchor; and (2) the `wordsOf` tokenizer incorrectly split terms like 'DigestSchema' into 'igest' and 'chema' due to uppercase letter treatment, breaking the schema structure. A revised anchor text with the clause 'leave other sections alone' improved T7 and T2 metrics but introduced a new lag in T11, showing that recency and retention are in direct tension. The model now correctly identifies that T11 is a real threshold — a synopsis that is out of date but not fabricated, which the model previously failed to detect.

**structure** (823 runes)

> The work is structured around the generation of accurate, time-anchored digests that reflect the actual state of ongoing work. Key components include: (1) the prompt-level accounting rule that tracks open items and prevents fabrication of closure states; (2) the anchor text configuration, which determines the recency bias of the synopsis; (3) the tokenizer pipeline, which processes text into measurable metrics; and (4) the metrics system, which evaluates retention, fabricated blockers, and lag. These parts interact: the anchor text influences recency, which affects retention and fabricated blockers, while the tokenizer integrity ensures that schema and other terms are preserved. The system currently fails when the anchor text overemphasizes recency at the cost of retention or when the tokenizer breaks key terms.

**insights** (8 entries)

1. The use of color to encode input vs. output provides a clear visual distinction that enhances user understanding of the model's behavior.
2. Provenance is best expressed through design, not metadata decoration — the structure itself becomes the documentation.
3. The presence of synthetic sessions shows that the work is focused on structural validity rather than factual accuracy.
4. The budget table reveals that the allocation of value to 'happened' is driven by contextual reasoning, not arbitrary thresholds.
5. Recency and retention are in direct tension: increasing focus on recent turns improves fabricated blocker rates and reduces retention, while reducing recency bias leads to outdated synopses that fail to reflect current work.
6. The model's reliance on `WithEnrichment` fields as a recency anchor is flawed because those fields are never processed in the digest path, resulting in a lack of present-oriented context.
7. The tokenizer `wordsOf` introduces structural damage when uppercase letters are treated as separators, fragmenting key terms like 'DigestSchema' — a flaw that only manifests in specific contexts and was previously undetected.
8. T11 lag is not a fabrication or misclassification — it is a genuine failure of the synopsis to reflect current work, which the model previously failed to identify as a distinct issue.

**current** (249 runes)

> The work is now focused on refining the digest generation logic to improve accuracy in tracking open items and preventing fabrication of closure states, particularly in long-running sessions where subject drift and recency bias create misalignments.

**why** (147 runes)

> To produce digests that are reliable, accurate, and grounded in the actual work being done — not in a biased or fabricated view of recent activity.

**next** (415 runes)

> 1. Implement a classification pass that includes `WithEnrichment` fields to provide a true recency anchor in the digest generation pipeline. 2. Replace `wordsOf` with a tokenizer that preserves case and term integrity, ensuring proper parsing of schema and other structured terms. 3. Conduct a controlled experiment to test the impact of the new anchor text on T4, T7, and T11 metrics across 10 additional sessions.

**unresolved** (3 entries)

1. The recency-retention trade-off remains unresolved — no configuration has yet been found that improves both retention and reduces lag in T11 without degrading other metrics.
2. The classification pass that would enable `WithEnrichment` fields to be used as a recency anchor has not been implemented and is not yet tested.
3. The tokenizer `wordsOf` has not been replaced with a case-preserving variant, and its impact on term integrity in schema fields remains unvalidated.

**The design, in short.** Two grains within the session — specific actions (recent window, in detail) and the session story (accumulating, coarsening as it grows). Between them a compression step: the refinement receives a **≤600-rune paraphrase** of the previous digest plus the deterministic retain-list, instead of 4,742 characters of embedded prose. That's your sentence exactly — *"work has been on X, Y, Z; specifically A, B, C"* — with the paraphrase supplying the framing and the retain-list supplying the instances.

**The invariant that makes it safe: store full, feed compressed.** My one hard-won finding is that repeated re-summarization erodes the best content. That still holds, so the lossy path is the *prompt* only. The stored digest is never regenerated from a paraphrase. The spec calls this out as needing a test rather than a convention, because it's the one way this design could quietly destroy the record.

**Three things it deletes.** The "must not become shorter" rule, which directly contradicts deliberate compression. `CarryForward` and the priority scheme deciding which sections yield budget.…
user: But to understand the larger picture of the session, would we not want to consult the summarized/condensed digests at some sampling frequency across the session or at least across a much larger rolling window?
assistant: Yes — and that's a real gap in what I wrote. A single paraphrase of the immediately-previous digest is a chain where each step sees only one step back, which is precisely the telephone risk I listed and then didn't actually mitigate. Consulting a *series* of condensed digests across the session both gives the trajectory and bounds the drift, because a late generation can see where the work started, not just where it was last round.

`digeststore` already keeps every snapshot with its `seq`, so the sequence is there to read.

**The story ladder.** Each refinement now receives a chronological sequence of stored paraphrases rather than just the last:

- **the first, always** — where the work started, so the account can say what the current work grew out of; dropping it is how a session loses its own origin
- **the most recent in full** (≤600 runes) — the immediate handover
- **evenly spaced middles, clipped short** (≤140 runes each) — the trajectory, without paying full price per step
- capped at **8**; beyond that the middles are resampled rather than appended

Dense at the recent end, sparse toward the start — the same shape `SessionDigest` already uses for turns, for the same reason.

**It's cheaper than what it replaces.** Worst case ~1,580 runes against the 4,742 the embedded digest costs, while covering the whole session instead of one step of it. That's the part I'd missed: sampling across the session isn't an added cost, it's what compression pays for.

**And it's the drift bound I claimed but hadn't built.** With a ladder, framing is checkable against the session's *own* earlier framings, so drift is visible to the generation that would otherwise compound it.…

## What was wrong
The page-header `actions` slot mixed two button sizes:
- Shared `HeaderActionButton` → `size="sm"` (the tinted pills: "New team", "Request an integration")
- Primary CTAs → plain `<Button>` at the default `md` ("Invite members", "New … Dimension")

Side by side, `sm` (32px) next to `md` (~40px) → the mismatch you saw.

## The fix (at the shared-component level, so it's uniform everywhere)
- **`components/header-action-button.tsx`** — added an `emphasis="primary" | "secondary"` prop. Both render at `size="sm"`, so *every* header action shares one height. `secondary` (default) keeps the tinted-pill look; `primary` is the filled green CTA.

- **`app/(app)/dimensions/page.tsx`** — "New … Dimension" likewise.

The integrations pages already used `HeaderActionButton`, so they were consistent; now the primary CTAs join them. Height is now governed solely by `size` (and the tertiary variant's border is inside the box, so it adds no height).
